title: A Gravity for the Archive
premise: Tamsin Zhou, an insurance investigator who has spent seven years certifying 'impossible accidents' in contested orbit, is assigned to a claim that shouldn't exist: a cargo hauler's manifest lists passengers the colony's records insist were never born. When the colony's children begin sharing one dream — a burning settlement on a moon that official history says was never settled — Tamsin realizes the dream is an inherited memory, and that her own late mother's name appears in it. To prove the Meridian Flats massacre happened, she must reconstruct evidence from smuggled keepsakes, corrupted black boxes, and the children's testimony, while the orbital consortium that owns every archive moves to erase the last witnesses. In the end, Tamsin broadcasts the reconstructed record from a decommissioned relay, forcing an open tribunal outside consortium law; justice arrives not as punishment but as recognition — the dead are entered into the archive at last, and Tamsin finally claims her own inheritance: her mother's true story, and a place in the community she'd only ever insured.
about_author: Quentin Thornbury is a former maritime claims adjuster who turned to science fiction after a decade of investigating losses no one wanted to explain. He writes from a houseboat in the Salish Sea, where he collects obsolete data formats and stories about things officially forgotten.

chapters.title: Actuarial Grace
chapters.summary: Tamsin Zhou certifies another impossible accident — a hull breach ruled 'operator error' — and pockets her fee. POV: Tamsin. The beat is weary competence masking numbness; she has learned to make tragedy legible to ledgers without letting it touch her.

chapters.title: The Claim That Shouldn't Exist
chapters.summary: A widow files for loss-of-life benefits naming a husband the colony registry says never existed. Tamsin investigates, finding his face in crew photos that have been doctored. POV: Tamsin. Emotional beat: the first crack in her faith in records — someone has been deleted, not just dead.

chapters.title: Children of the Shared Dream
chapters.summary: Across the station, forty children wake describing the same fire on Meridian Flats, down to the smell of ionized regolith. A teacher begs Tamsin to look. POV: alternating Tamsin and nine-year-old Idris. Beat: uncanny dread; the past is speaking through people too young to lie convincingly.

chapters.title: Black Box, White Noise
chapters.summary: Tamsin recovers a corrupted flight recorder from a salvage yard; its final minutes show a settlement burning under deliberate strafing. The timestamp predates the moon's official habitation by eleven years. POV: Tamsin. Beat: cold exhilaration curdling into fear as she realizes what the evidence implies.

chapters.title: Her Mother's Name
chapters.summary: Cross-referencing the recorder's passenger list, Tamsin finds 'L. Zhou' — her mother, who died when Tamsin was six, officially a dock clerk. POV: Tamsin, with flashback fragments. Beat: grief reopened; the investigation becomes personal inheritance.

chapters.title: The Consortium's Courtesy
chapters.summary: An insurance executive offers Tamsin a promotion and a quiet request to close the file. She declines; within hours her clearance drops and her berth lease is flagged. POV: Tamsin. Beat: the machinery of erasure turns its attention to her — menace delivered politely.

chapters.title: Idris Remembers Dying
chapters.summary: Idris describes the dream's ending in first person — running, falling — and draws a door with a yellow stencil. Tamsin recognizes the stencil from the wreck. POV: Idris. Beat: heartbreak and horror; a child carrying a dead adult's final moments.

chapters.title: The Keepsake Network
chapters.summary: Tamsin tracks survivors' descendants who secretly preserved contraband relics: a scorched toy, a hand-written ledger, a wedding ring. Each object contradicts the official record. POV: Tamsin. Beat: cautious hope; a hidden community of memory reveals itself.

chapters.title: Orbital Law Is Consortium Law
chapters.summary: Tamsin petitions the colonial magistrate; the case is dismissed for lack of standing — you cannot sue over people who never lived. Her ally, advocate Ruth Okafor, proposes an old maritime remedy: a public inquiry convened outside corporate charter. POV: Ruth. Beat: legal ingenuity against institutional wall.

chapters.title: Sabotage
chapters.summary: Tamsin's skiff suffers a 'random' guidance failure; she survives a brutal manual reentry. The consortium denies involvement. POV: Tamsin. Beat: terror and resolve — they've moved from pressure to attempted murder.

chapters.title: What the Children Know Together
chapters.summary: Ruth deposes the children; their overlapping details form a map accurate to terrain Tamsin verifies physically on Meridian Flats — foundations, a mass grave site, the yellow-stenciled door. POV: Tamsin and Idris. Beat: awe; testimony becomes geography becomes proof.

chapters.title: The Archivist Who Kept Nothing
chapters.summary: Tamsin finds the retired consortium archivist, Vey, living in exile. He confesses he was ordered to purge Meridian Flats but couldn't destroy everything — he hid fragments inside deprecated formats no one reads anymore. POV: Vey. Beat: guilt seeking redemption; the keeper of erasure becomes its undoing.

chapters.title: Deprecated Formats
chapters.summary: In Vey's storage, Tamsin decodes tape archives: video of the massacre, names of 312 dead, and her mother's voice narrating the final evacuation order. POV: Tamsin. Beat: devastating intimacy — hearing a dead parent speak truth into the dark.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: The consortium escalates: full amnesty for the descendants, reparations, and Tamsin's mother posthumously honored — if the children's testimony is sealed and the massacre attributed to a long-defunct pirate faction. POV: Tamsin. Beat: temptation; justice as a purchase price.

chapters.title: What Belonging Costs
chapters.summary: The descendant community splits — some want the settlement, others the truth. Idris's father votes to take the deal; Idris refuses, saying the dream-children didn't survive so their deaths could be reassigned. POV: Idris. Beat: moral clarity from the smallest voice; the community fractures.

chapters.title: Seizure
chapters.summary: Consortium agents raid Vey's storage and Ruth's office; the tapes vanish, Vey is detained, Ruth is disbarred on fabricated charges. Tamsin escapes with one copied fragment. POV: Tamsin. Beat: despair at the nadir — every institution has closed around her.

chapters.title: The Relay
chapters.summary: Tamsin remembers a decommissioned comm relay she once inspected — still licensed, technically, to broadcast. If she can reach it, she can transmit the surviving fragment plus the children's mapped testimony colony-wide before the license lapses in sixty hours. POV: Tamsin. Beat: desperate plan; the last unowned channel.

chapters.title: Sixty Hours
chapters.summary: A cat-and-mouse run through contested orbits as consortium patrol ships sweep the relay corridor. Descendants who chose truth smuggle Tamsin fuel and decoy transponders. POV: Tamsin. Beat: solidarity forged under fire; the community chooses itself.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: From the relay, Tamsin transmits her mother's voice, the grave-site coordinates, and the children's testimony live. Across the colony, adults begin dreaming the fire too — memory refusing containment once witnessed. POV: multiple, mosaic. Beat: catharsis; the archive breaks open.

chapters.title: The Tribunal of the Unrecorded
chapters.summary: Under public pressure, an independent tribunal convenes under maritime law. Vey testifies; the consortium's cover-up unravels; Meridian Flats's 312 dead are formally entered into the colonial register. POV: Ruth. Beat: justice achieved — imperfect, procedural, real.

chapters.title: Names Read Aloud
chapters.summary: At a memorial on Meridian Flats, the names are read; Idris places a yellow-stenciled door on the grave site. Tamsin learns her mother died shielding evacuees — a heroism the record now holds forever. POV: Tamsin and Idris. Beat: mourning transmuted into belonging.

chapters.title: A Gravity for the Archive
chapters.summary: Months later, Tamsin resigns from insurance work to run the colony's new independent archive, teaching children how records lie and how to catch them. The shared dreams fade gently, leaving only ordinary memories. POV: Tamsin. Beat: quiet resolution — she stops insuring the past and starts keeping it.
